analysis.statement: HyDE’s reliance on a single instruction‑following LLM to generate hypothetical documents may limit its ability to capture the specialized terminology and citation patterns typical of legal texts.
The assumption of a unimodal query embedding distribution (E3) could be especially problematic for legal queries, which often encode multiple sub‑questions (e.g., facts, statutes, precedents).

Because HyDE’s contrastive encoder is trained only on document‑only data without relevance signals (E10), it may not learn the nuanced relevance judgments that legal practitioners apply (e.g., binding vs. persuasive authority).
The averaging of N sampled hypothetical documents (E4) may dilute rare but critical legal concepts, reducing recall for niche statutes or case law.

HyDE performs well in zero‑shot settings across diverse domains (E6, E7), suggesting that with domain‑specific prompt engineering it could achieve competitive retrieval for legal corpora without supervised fine‑tuning.

directions.title: Legal‑Prompted HyDE (LP‑HyDE)
directions.rationale: Customizing the instruction (INST) to include legal‑specific cues (e.g., "generate a brief legal memorandum addressing the query") may steer the LLM to produce hypothetical documents that embed domain terminology and citation style, improving query embedding quality for legal search.
directions.validation_experiment: Dataset: COLIEE 2023 legal case retrieval; Baseline: standard HyDE with generic prompt; Metric: nDCG@10 and recall@1k; Compare LP‑HyDE vs. baseline.

directions.title: Multi‑Modal Query Embedding for Ambiguous Legal Queries
directions.rationale: Legal queries often contain multiple intents (e.g., factual background + statutory interpretation). Extending HyDE to generate a set of diverse hypothetical documents (instead of averaging) can capture a multimodal embedding space, addressing the limitation noted in E3/E12.
directions.validation_experiment: Dataset: LegalBench QA with multi‑intent queries; Baseline: original HyDE (averaged embedding); Metric: MAP and query‑intent coverage (precision@5 for each intent).

directions.title: Contrastive Encoder Fine‑Tuned on Legal Citation Networks
directions.rationale: While HyDE’s encoder is unsupervised (E10), injecting weak supervision from citation graphs (e.g., case‑to‑case citations) can teach the encoder the hierarchical relevance patterns of law without full relevance labels.
directions.validation_experiment: Dataset: Caselaw Access Project; Weak supervision: citation adjacency; Baseline: vanilla HyDE encoder; Metric: citation‑aware recall@1k and nDCG@10.

directions.title: Dynamic Sampling Count for Rare Legal Concepts
directions.rationale: Increasing N for queries containing rare legal terms may prevent dilution of critical signals (E4). An adaptive sampler that raises N when term frequency is low could improve recall for niche statutes.
directions.validation_experiment: Dataset: Statute retrieval benchmark with long‑tail terms; Baseline: fixed N=5; Adaptive N (1–20 based on term rarity); Metric: recall@100 for rare vs. common queries.

sources.text:
Concretely in this paper, we introduce a new paradigm of interactions between LLM and dense encoder/retriever. We demonstrate (part of) relevance modeling and instruction understanding can be delegated to the more powerful and flexible LLM. As a consequence, the need for relevance labels is removed. We are excited to see how this can be generalized further to more sophisticated tasks like multi-hop retrieval/QA and conversational search.

We argue HyDE is also of practical use though not necessarily over the entire lifespan of a search system. At the very beginning of the life of the search system, serving queries using HyDE offers performance comparable to a fine-tuned model, which no other relevance-free model can offer. As the search log grows, a supervised dense retriever can be gradually rolled out. As the dense retriever grows stronger, more queries will be routed to it, with only less common and emerging ones going to HyDE backend.

2 Related Works

Dense Retrieval (Lee et al., 2019; Karpukhin et al., 2020) has been extensively studied after the emergence of pre-trained Transformer language models (Devlin et al., 2019). Researchers studied the metric learning problems, such as training loss (Karpukhin et al., 2020) and negative sampling (Xiong et al., 2021; Qu et al., 2021), and also introduced distillation (Qu et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2021b; Hofstätter et al., 2021). Later works studied the second stage pre-training of language model specifically for retrieval (Izacard et al., 2021; Gao and Callan, 2021; Lu et al., 2021; Gao and Callan, 2022; Liu and Shao, 2022). The popularity of dense retrieval can be partially attributed to the rich and successful research in very efficient minimum inner product search (MIPS) at very large (billion) scales (Johnson et al., 2017).

3 Methodology

In this section, we first formally define the problem of (zero-shot) dense retrieval. Then we will introduce how HyDE is designed to solve it.

Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval The tasks of zeroshot (dense) retrieval are arguably empirically defined by Thakur et al. (2021) for the neural retrieval community. Their BEIR benchmark consists of diverse retrieval tasks. The paper and many follow-up research generally consider the Transfer Learning setup where the dense retriever is first learned using a diverse and richly supervised corpus and query collection, namely MS-MARCO (Thakur et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022).

However, as stated by Izacard et al. (2021), such a large collection can rarely be assumed. In this paper, therefore, we study the problem of building effective dense retrieval systems without relevance labels. Similar to Izacard et al. (2021), we also do not assume access to the test time corpora for training. This is a more realistic setup and prevents over-engineering on the test corpora.
